explanation:
## The division trap

```rust
fn bucket_of(&self, x: i64) -> Option<usize> {
    if x < self.lo { return None; }
    let i = ((x - self.lo) / self.width) as usize;
    if i < self.buckets.len() { Some(i) } else { None }
}
```

The early return is not tidiness. Without it, `x = -5` with `lo = 0` and
`width = 10` gives `(-5) / 10`, which in Rust truncates **towards zero**
and is therefore `0` — so the value lands in bucket 0 and is counted as
inside. Change the numbers to `x = -15` and the quotient is `-1`, and
`-1 as usize` is `18446744073709551615`. One of those is a silently
wrong answer and the other is an index that will not be less than
`buckets.len()`, so it happens to be caught; neither is a design.

Truncation towards zero is the C and Rust convention and it makes
negative-side bucketing wrong in a way that is easy to miss. Python
would floor instead, giving `-1` for `-5 / 10`, which is right for
bucketing and wrong for other things. Checking the lower bound before
dividing avoids having to know which language you are in.

## `&self`, `&mut self`, and calling one from the other

`add` takes `&mut self` and calls `bucket_of`, which takes `&self`.
That is fine: an exclusive borrow can be reborrowed as a shared one for
as long as the call lasts.

What does **not** compile is

```rust
self.buckets[self.bucket_of(x).unwrap()] += 1;   // no
```

because the index expression borrows `self` while the assignment is
already borrowing `self.buckets` mutably. Finishing the call first —
`let i = self.bucket_of(x);` and then indexing — makes the two borrows
consecutive rather than overlapping. The compiler is pointing at a real
rule, not being fussy; this is the same rule that makes aliasing bugs
impossible, and the fix is always to shorten one of the borrows.

## Saturating arithmetic

`saturating_add(1)` stops at `u32::MAX`. In release mode a plain `+= 1`
would wrap silently from `u32::MAX` to 0; in debug mode it would panic.
Neither is what a counter should do, and saying `saturating_add` makes
the decision visible at the point it is taken.

Rust makes you choose: `wrapping_add`, `checked_add`, `saturating_add`
and `overflowing_add` are four methods because there are four
reasonable answers and the language declines to guess.

## The mode, and why the empty case needs `Option`

```rust
let mut best: Option<usize> = None;
for (i, c) in self.buckets.iter().enumerate() {
    if *c > 0 && (best.is_none() || *c > self.buckets[best.unwrap()]) {
        best = Some(i);
    }
}
```

Two decisions. `*c > 0` means an all-empty histogram has no mode rather
than a mode of 0 — "bucket 0 is the fullest, with nothing in it" is not
a useful answer. And `>` rather than `>=` keeps the first of several
equal maxima, which is what the specification asks for.

Returning `Option<usize>` rather than a sentinel index such as
`usize::MAX` is the whole argument for having `Option` in the language:
the caller cannot use the answer without first saying what it will do
when there is not one, and the compiler checks that it did.
